content: Dilarang masuk tanpa izin dari petugas
keamanan gedung ini.
= No entry without permission from
this building's security officer.
There is no subject in that sentence, and
there is no need for one. Official
Indonesian is passive by habit: the deed
comes first and the doer is left out.
On a sign, that passive is a command.
Dilarang masuk.
= No entry.
Harap tenang.
= Please be quiet.
harus (must) and boleh (may) do the rest.
The register has its own vocabulary, and
this tier is where you meet it:
resmi          official
izin           permission
formulir       a form to fill in
identitas      identity
dengan hormat  respectfully
A letter opens with the reader's title,
never with a pronoun:
Kepada Yth. Bapak Budi Santoso
= To the honored Mr Budi Santoso
Yth. is short for yang terhormat, the one
who is honored - yang and ter- at their
ordinary work inside a fixed phrase.
Anda belongs here; kamu never does.
Januari   April  Juli       Oktober
Februari  Mei    Agustus    November
Maret     Juni   September  Desember
Like the days of Lesson 9, the months
take a capital letter. A date runs small
to large, and pada introduces it:
pada hari Senin, tanggal 17 Agustus
Kami merayakan Natal pada bulan Desember.
= We celebrate Christmas in December.
bulan means both month and moon:
bulan ini    this month
bulan Mei    in May
The counting words go further in this
tier:
juta      a million
persen    per cent
lusin     a dozen
puluhan   tens of, scores of
setengah, a half, you have had since
Tier 2:
Hampir setengah dari keluarga kami
tinggal di kota besar.
= Almost half our family live in the
city.
-an on a number makes it vague. puluhan
orang is tens of people, ratusan is
hundreds of them, ribuan is thousands.
Kepada Yth. Bapak Budi Santoso
= To Mr Budi Santoso (on a letter)
Indonesians address one another by title
far more than by name, and almost never
by a bare pronoun. Get the title right
and Anda becomes unnecessary.
Bapak -> Pak  a man older or senior
Ibu   -> Bu   a woman, likewise
Kakak -> Kak  a little older than you
Adik  -> Dik  a little younger
The full form is written; the short form
is spoken.
Pak, ini punya Bapak?              Press 1
= Sir, is this yours?
Two more you will hear all day, and which
no card in this pack carries:
Mas   a young man, very common in Java
Mbak  a young woman, likewise
Use them in a shop, at a stall, in a taxi.
They are polite, warm and safe.
Three on the cards are dated, and their
notes say so. Tuan, Nyonya and Nona
belong to old letters and old films.
Saudara is formal and a little cool:
right on a form, chilly at a table.
The rule of thumb: when you do not know
what to call someone, Pak or Bu is never
wrong, and a bare name almost always is.
